## TL;DR

The Agents page's model Test action could report only a short status badge after
a failed probe. The diagnostic lived in a native title tooltip, so the action
did not clearly explain how to recover from a missing CLI, expired sign-in, or
provider rate limit. I added shared classification for missing executables and
rendered failure guidance inline in an accessible status region. Unit and
component tests cover all three cases, and a headless browser run confirmed the
messages on the Agents page with deterministic API fixtures. The required
changed-path RepoOS check passed on the formatted tree.

## Work and rationale

I started by tracing the failure path from the Agents card's Test button through
`POST /api/models/test` and the model-test runner, then checked the shared
agent-failure classifier and existing last-run failure UI. The backend already
returned the correct high-level status and retained diagnostic text for failed
probes. Authentication and quota messages were already recognized by the
shared classifier, but missing executables were not a named failure category.
At the component layer the button showed “failed” while exposing the error only
through a `title` attribute. That made the information inaccessible until a
hover and relied on the browser's native tooltip for essential guidance.

I extended the shared classifier with a `missing-cli` reason for `ENOENT`,
“could not launch”, “command not found”, and “no such file or directory”
diagnostics. The resulting message names the selected CLI and directs the user
to install it and ensure its executable is on PATH. The existing auth and
usage-limit reasons provide their established, actionable guidance. In
`AgentCard`, I now derive concise feedback from the failure and render it under
the compatibility action as a visible `role="status"` message. The status
badge remains, and the native title tooltip is removed so the explanation is
present in the page's accessible text instead of only browser chrome. The new
message styling follows the existing muted text and uses the global stylesheet.

The classifier tests assert the missing-CLI reason and its install/PATH fix.
The AgentsView component test clicks Test with representative missing-executable,
signed-out, and rate-limited payloads. It verifies that the action settles on
“failed”, the matching recovery guidance is visible inside a status region, and
the failure does not use a title tooltip. These tests exercise the button's
request/result flow and the same helper used to classify stored run failures.

For the browser pass, I ran `just serve-noauth 7272` from the task worktree,
loaded `/agents?shotState=agents:lastRuns` in headless Playwright Chromium, and
intercepted only the model-test endpoint with deterministic responses. The
missing-executable case showed that OpenCode could not be found and how to
install it; the authentication case asked the user to re-authenticate; and the
HTTP 429 case explained the provider limit and said to wait before retrying.
The card showed the failed state for each response and the browser recorded no
page errors. The local server was stopped after the run.

## Approaches tried

I first inspected whether the underlying runner or API discarded the failure.
It did not: the API returned a result with the `failed` status and diagnostic
string, so changing the route or altering the model probe would have duplicated
existing behavior. I also checked the detected-agent view, where missing
installations already have a separate “not installed” indicator. That panel is
useful for discovery, but it does not explain a failed compatibility test on
the configured card, so I kept the fix on the Test result path.

The implemented approach reuses `classifyAgentFailure` for user-facing copy
instead of building a second set of auth and rate-limit rules in the Vue
component. The Test endpoint continues to return diagnostic details unchanged;
the UI classifies them for display. This keeps raw runner behavior intact and
lets the card present a brief next step. For failures outside known classes,
the component falls back to the returned error string so the UI does not hide a
diagnostic it cannot classify.

## Challenges and blockers

The first required scoped check reported a formatting failure in the new
classifier change. As directed by the repository check instructions, I ran
`bun run fmt` and reran `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check`. The first
remote validation passed its build, changed-path tests, rendered contrast, and
UI smoke, but the surrounding check was interrupted while entering local
guards. I ran the complete scoped check again to establish a final result.
That run passed the remote validation and the local guards, including format,
lint, build staleness, contrast, and UI smoke. The remote test run reported
4,566 passing tests and one skipped test.

The browser responses were fixtures rather than live provider requests. This
was intentional for a deterministic QA pass and avoided making claims about
credentials or real provider quota state. The checked behavior is how the page
renders representative API failures. A real provider's exact diagnostic text
and a real account's authentication state remain outside this run's evidence.

## Key learnings

The model compatibility API was already accurately distinguishing a failed
probe, but the card's status-only presentation made failure feedback feel
incomplete. Returning a status is only useful if the next step is discoverable
at the point of failure. Reusing a classifier already responsible for agent
failure messages also avoids differences between the Test action and run
history for the same failure class.

For “missing CLI”, a low-level spawn error is technically accurate but does not
help a user resolve it. Naming installation and PATH as the two likely fixes
makes the failure actionable without changing CLI detection or pretending
that the CLI is authenticated. For sign-in and quota errors, the existing
classifier already offers appropriate next steps, so the missing piece was
making those steps visible and accessible on the card. The fixture-based
browser pass is useful evidence for rendering and interaction, while the
report distinguishes that from verification against real provider accounts.
